utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Good morning, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours this the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. All the accused are here, and were it not for Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Haynes we would be full house. But we aren't. And from the Prosecution I notice Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, and Mr. Vanderpuye. Is there anyone else? All right. I take it there are no preliminaries? We might come back to you on a couple of points later. We need to finish with the documents, the Defence team for Popovic, in relation to the previous witness. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We provided the list of our documents and distributed to the all teams and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And are there any objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not right now, Mr. President. A few of them were not dealt with with the witness, but we've spoken to Mr. Zivanovic, and we all think they are part of his report. If there's a problem there we'll let you know, but I don't think there should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you dealt with that last time. Basically you said that they referred to the witness's report or something like that and in view of that you would not be objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was the Nikolic team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think the situation is the same, but the Prosecution has one additional document it to offer, and that is 1D1302. That's the Matowietsky Report that Mr. Zivanovic said he was going to offer at the time. He's - I've spoken to him. He's changed his mind, but given that it was used and why it was used and how it was used, we -- I would offer that report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think one of the reasons my learned friend Mr. Zivanovic didn't use it is I made it clear to him that I would oppose it if he sought to put it in. I haven't had that conversation with Mr. McCloskey. He wasn't aware of it. I take the same stance. Two paragraphs of a very long report was referred to. Those two paragraphs were read out. They could be exhibited separately, and I would take no objection to that. But why the rest of the report should go in I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were the two paragraphs part of the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I used just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but they were part of the conclusions in other words. Yes, one moment Mr. McCloskey. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully support what Mr. Josse just said, but would I like to add that this is a very long document and it deals with '93, the year '93, which is not really relevant [as interpreted] in this trial. Furthermore, I believe that the Trial Chamber has a practice when there are only two paragraphs that were presented, and when these paragraphs have already been read out during the hearing there's no need to tender the full document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 1993 is of significant relevance to this case. The history of this situation is vitally important to understand. We have chosen to target our indictment to 1995, but that has not kept anyone from dealing in depth with 1993. This witness dealt in depth with 1992, 1993, and we heard document after document, statement after statement of the situation with Naser Oric and the 28th Division. And then the Matowietsky Report is used for one particular conclusion, so I bring the Matowietsky Report in because the Defence used it for a conclusion in a report and to rebut much of what the witness said. You know, the Defence brings up these sorts of things at their peril, and you can't just take one little piece and then expect that that little piece is going to sit by itself. And the paragraph above their piece was also obviously very important, but those two important conclusions are not fully in context unless you see the whole report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are obviously eight parties to this case, seven accused, and perhaps the Chamber would bear that in mind in relation to what Mr. McCloskey has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Otherwise -- yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just to add the Borovcanin Defence would like to draw in the objection that my learned colleague Mr. Josse has raised and also what Madam Fauveau has just said. It was in the line of this Trial Chamber, so only what was used during cross-examination of the witness should enter into evidence, not the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We join, as well, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Even that the 1993 events are not relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, and I watch that very carefully, and I'm happy that my learned friend was open and honest with the Court regarding that. I do not share -- I agree with my learned friend the 1993 is relevant and it is probative as the Court knows from our evidence, and I'm glad that he agrees with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our decision is as follows: We are not yet in a position to know precisely whether for our purposes when we come to deliberate having in the records just that one page where -- which was made use of would suffice or not. It may well be the case that in order to understand better that conclusion, we might need to refer to the rest of the report or other parts of that report. So our decision is, for the time being, we are admitting that page only with the caveat that if we feel the need to have the whole report, UN report, admitted, then we will ask for it, and of course we will let you know that we have done so. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry I was not more prepared on that issue. I thought Mr. Zivanovic was going to offer it into evidence. It is a 20-page report only, and would the Court accept a brief argument from the Prosecution on that? When I take a closer look at that last page, maybe there is a way to narrow it down to the chapter or whatever, But it's only a 20-page report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Ms. -- let's not lose more time on this. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to correct the transcript. On page 2, last line, line 25, or page 3, first line, 1993 was not -- it says that "1993 was not relevant." It's not exactly what I said. I said that 1993 is not the topic of this trial, which is a bit different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's important. So all these documents of the Popovic Defence team are admitted. I take it there are no objections from any of the other Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems that quite a number of them have not yet been translated, and therefore, those will remain marked for identification only until they are translated to the satisfaction of the parties, and then the upgrade will be automatic. With regard to the document that the Prosecution tendered, I think we have been clear. It's only that page which is being received for the time being. The rest we'll decide if we need afterwards. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm told that's page 18 from that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Page 18. Thank you. So we have now finished the first Defence case, and we are starting with the second today. In the meantime, before I give the floor to Mr. Beara, there is a motion from the Nikolic Defence team which I would kindly ask you to attend to and come back to us at your earliest, please, with your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That will be done with all the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And Mr. Ostojic. You have 60 minutes. Defence Opening Statement:

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. May it please the Court, my learned friends from both sides of the table, Mr. Beara and other accused. Your Honours, it is certainly a privilege after two years to be able to have an opportunity again to address you, and once again, on behalf of the Beara Defence we thank you for that opportunity. We've heard a lot of evidence, but I think we have not heard a sufficient amount of evidence. My preliminary remarks are that proof that crimes have been -- have occurred or that they have been committed is not sufficient to sustain a conviction of an individual. Criminal proceedings require much more, and they require that the Prosecution establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused is responsible for crimes before a conviction can be entered. I raise that because the issue of burden of proof comes to mind, and we must remind ourselves once again that we, the Defence, have no burden whatsoever to prove any element or any facts in this case. The burden of proof as decided by the decisional authority in this Tribunal is that it remains with the Prosecution throughout the trial, even the phase of the Defence case. That burden, as heavy as it may be, which is to prove beyond a reasonable doubt, is a cardinal principle of criminal law. The burden never shifts to the accused or the Defence, and by choosing to present evidence during this phase of the proceedings, we are not suggesting or intimating that we are accepting or shifting that burden to ourselves; but rather, it is a further step in the process and the interest of justice to assist this honourable Trial Chamber to see the areas and issues which have not been proven beyond a reasonable doubt And to show the Trial Chamber where certain reasonable inferences may be drawn in favour of the accused. The first issue I'd like to discuss and establish with the evidence that we'll bring is the issue between evacuation and deportation or forcible transfer. In paragraph 78 of the second amended consolidated indictment, the Prosecution alleges against Mr. Beara that he planned, organised, and assisted in the gathering together, detaining, and transporting of Muslim men. They further allege that he supervised, facilitated, and oversaw the men from Potocari that they be placed in detention centres in the Zvornik area. What evidence do we expect to bring forth and why? Initially, I must tell the Court that one of our witnesses, although she is a joint witness, is a demographer, Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic. She will hopefully come during our case, as we've identified her on the list of witnesses for July to assist, the Trial Chamber and to show us that defects and the flaws in the OTP's demographic analysis through experts which they have brought. We also believe that through her testimony she will further reveal not only the flaws in that analysis but the flaws used in the methodology and the conclusions reached by the demographic experts that the OTP provided to the Court. We believe that her evidence will assist us in giving us more accurately the number of citizens and the population that existed in Srebrenica at that critical time. In keeping things in context, I think it's important to know whether those citizens in Srebrenica were themselves refugees and whether or not the government of BiH at any time and specifically in 1993, expressly as we've seen from time to time, prohibited them from exiting Srebrenica. Their willingness or voluntariness to leave will be an issue that will be discussed as some length. The movement or removal of the civilians in cooperation with DutchBat was an evacuation in our opinion and as a result a military necessity and was not either deportation or forcible transfer. When we see the allegations in paragraph 78 of this second amended consolidated indictment, we look again at the words that they have alleged of planned, organised, and assisted. Although I must say that I believe the OTP evidence is not only doubtful, it doesn't exist in that regard with respect to Mr. Beara. A key focus for us, and I think this Tribunal, should be the whereabouts of Mr. Beara during these critical time periods. We know several things that the OTP did during their investigation and during the presentation of their evidence as well as through witnesses that they brought forth here at trial, and they acknowledge that they have no evidence whatsoever of Ljubisa Beara's whereabouts from July 16th through July 31st, 1995, and I believe that in January of this year Mr. Butler plainly and reasonably said so. In addition, the OTP, when it comes to Mr. Beara, although they make these vast allegations, have no evidence whatsoever as to his whereabouts from July 1st through July 11th inclusive, 1995. Given that, when we look at the allegations there is no such evidence with respect to planning, organising, or assisting. The evidence was not brought forth, and once again it is not our burden to share with the Court where the whereabouts of Mr. Beara, was but there should be enough reasonable doubt and lack of evidence to acquit simply by the evidence that they brought forth and/or lack thereof. Nevertheless, in the interests of justice and in the spirit of having this Court have evidence that we believe is probative and relevant, we bring forth evidence and, again, although not our duty and certainly not our burden, to show, reveal, and expose the weaknesses in the OTP's theory. Evidence will be called and has been heard that the VRS at that time was divided into six geographical-based corps in a very vast territory. The 1st Krajina corps, the 2nd Krajina corps, the Sarajevo-Romania corps, the Herzegovina corps, the east Bosnia corps, as well as from what we know from this trial, the Drina Corps. We asked the question, would the VRS or any military and its Main Staff, despite the spring 1995 offensive in the Krajina areas and in the Birac area, simply ignore who fail to send any of its staff officers to those regions during July 1995? We know briefly the answer to that question because the Office of the Prosecution brought one witness, Mihajlo Milovanovic, who is the Chief of Staff, and he states that he was on the other front, namely in the Birac area or in the east Bosnia corps. We have evidence and we hope to present evidence and expect to present that evidence to you that from July 16th for approximately 10 to 12 days, Mr. Beara went to various subordinate corps in the VRS throughout that vast territory including the 1st Krajina corps, the 2nd Krajina corps, and the east Bosnia corps. According to the Prosecution, no one went to that area even though there was a war brewing and combat engagements existing on all the fronts, both east and west, as well as north and south. It would be unrealistic to believe that the entirety of the Main Staff or the entirety of the VRS was concentrated in the enclave of Srebrenica and/or Zepa. The evidence will be elicited from people who were at these various subordinate corps as well as from, we expect, Mr. Ljubisa Beara's driver, Milos Tomovic. I must spend some time to discuss this witness with the Court. Mr. Beara's driver was interviewed by the OTP on one occasion. We heard that briefly from their lead investigator at the time, Tomas, Tomas Blascyk, and he indeed informed the Office of the Prosecution of the whereabouts of Mr. Beara. He informed them that he drove Mr. Beara both to the 1st, 2nd, and east -- 1st, 2nd Krajina corps and the east Bosnia corps as well. Why their investigator and why their analysts were not privy to that information will be a discussion that we will submit to this Court at a later time, namely during closing arguments. They have had this information for a long time, and yet they don't utilize it, but they leave us in the dark. Similarly, the Office of the Prosecution knew or should have known that when a very frightened and scared individual with no counsel or representation and absolutely no preparation erroneously states under oath on the record that he himself was never in Belgrade on July 13th or 14th, 1995, we believe that it is the duty of the Prosecution, having all the evidence that they have seized in their possession to assist this witness to obtain a clear and honest record. Mr. Tomovic in his interview states that he was not in Belgrade in July 13th, 1995, which is simply not true. How do we know? When assisted to refresh his recollection, and this is evidence we hope and expect that you will hear, when Mr. Tomovic was assisted and his recollection refreshed, he recalled and verified that indeed he was in Belgrade on July 13th, 1995 on the order of Zdravko Tolimir. Seems simple enough, but it becomes more complicated. As I am sure all are thinking how was is and what was used to refresh his recollection? Again, we used evidence that was in the possession of the OTP to assist and to probe and to find the truth of the matter. We asked initially Mr. Tomovic whether he kept a diary; he said no. But we found the diary, and it was not the diary of Mr. Beara or Mr. Tomovic but it was a diary of an American journalist from Phoenix, Arizona, of Serbian decent. This American journalist was also interviewed by the Office of the Prosecution in his diary that he kept contemporaneously with the visits that he had in the Srebrenica, Belgrade, and Pale and Sarajevo areas were in July of 1995. He took down daily records of people that he met, who drove him, where they drove him from. This daily record indicates on the date of July 13th that Mr. Robert Djurdjevic from Phoenix, Arizona, the American journalist I referred to, was picked up by Milos Tomovic. When we inquired of Mr. Tomovic if he has a recollection of that American journalist, he said he did, but he couldn't remember the dates. He said, I remember picking up an American Serb from Belgrade and drove him down to Vlasenica because he was required and insisted on having a meeting with General Mladic. On the cover of this diary and then also in the diary as my learned friends know, this journalist in detailed fashion shows where Mr. Tomovic drove him, what they observed, where the checkpoints were, and whom they encountered with. On the cover of that diary, I believe that it says written by the journalist himself, that this diary should not be opened or disclosed for two to three years until after the war in the former Yugoslavia ceases. This diary was created at the time and kept contemporaneous with the events that have occurred and unlike other documents was not at any time in anybody's possession but the Office of the Prosecution and was not altered or manipulated with. When we initially met with Mr. Tomovic, we asked, do you remember anything else; are you sure that it was the 13th? He couldn't. When we showed him the diary, although it is in English and we translated it for him and showed him the specific dates that were conspicuous on the diary, his first reaction was, oh, my God; that means that I lied to the Prosecution when I told them I never went to Belgrade on the 13th of July, 1995. Mr. Tomovic never lied to the Prosecution when he was interviewed. Mr. Tomovic was scared. Mr. Tomovic as most witnesses when they are confronted with the Prosecution request to talk about events that are horrific and tragic was certainly intimidated. Mr. Tomovic made a mistake. The support to confirm that Mr. Tomovic actually was in Belgrade in July 13th, 1995, is independent, and it should be accepted by this Court without debate. The rest of the story, of course, deals directly with the whereabouts of Mr. Beara. Milan Stanic, our investigator, and Milos Tomovic will address those issues: Who drove with Milos Tomovic when he went to Belgrade? Who else but the person that Mr. Tomovic normally and regularly drives? When we look in the context of what was happening July 12th, the Muslim men escaped to the forest unbeknownst to the VRS, unbeknownst to the Drina Corps. The Drina Corps find themselves in a situation where they are not engaged in battle in Srebrenica itself. The 12th negotiations were being conducted to evacuate the civilian population with DutchBat in participation. For most parts, the event of Srebrenica occurred quickly, quietly, and it was over. Of course, Mr. Beara's birthday is the 14th of July. We've discussed that on numerous occasions or at least in our last opening two years ago. Mr. Beara had reason to go to Belgrade, and the evidence we produce will help illustrate those reasons and where he was specifically on that day. Now, we know and we understand that mere presence or absence at the scene of a crime does not render a person either culpable or innocent, especially given the overly broad and in my opinion rather diluted theory of Joint Criminal Enterprise that the Prosecution alleges against us. Nevertheless, we firmly believe that the whereabouts of Mr. Beara and, indeed, significantly while addressing the issues of planning, organising, and assisting become all the more important. I'm not sure if Mr. President is indicating for me to stop. Okay. Thank you. The evidence is consistent in this regard as to Mr. Beara's whereabouts, and we've seen even from the presentation of the evidence that the Prosecution called that Mr. Beara was not seen ever in Srebrenica, and we can take a look at any of those videos. He was never seen in Potocari, and we have those videos as well. He was never seen at the Hotel Fontana at either the first, second, or third meeting; And certainly, he wasn't even seen at Mr. Zivanovic's retirement party. It's significant for many reasons. The obvious one, he wasn't seen because he was not there. He physically was not in that area or territory during that time period. It's also significant because we believe that it shows what I referenced two years ago, a detachment that Mr. Beara was not within a close knit group and did not follow Mladic or others and was excluded particularly from key and relevant situations. In fact, I believe our first witness today will testify about this detachment and will give the Court some background on it because keeping it in context is relevant and should be permitted. Before the VRS was formed, the Court should understand where Mr. Beara was and who was his subordinate. For example, this next witness we hope will establish for the Court that as late as 1990 and 1991, Mr. Zdravko Tolimir was a subordinate to Mr. Beara. When Mr. Tolimir goes to the VRS and several months later - approximately six, if I'm correct - Mr. Beara joins the VRS and he becomes not a superior or doesn't remain a superior to Mr. Tolimir; he becomes his subordinate, despite the fact that Mr. Tolimir is nine to ten years younger than Mr. Beara. And all of us who have studied any military code and know anything about rank can appreciate the significance of that evidence and the import that it has, and in our view, the relevance it has as to why Mr. Beara was indeed detached from General Mladic and others. Naturally, the VRS was a newly formed army, and it had numerous conflicts within itself as well as the political parties and the pro-Serbian nationalists, both for power, position, and rank within their territory. The dislike or the displeasure, lack of trust and lack of cooperation, and quite candidly, the lack of relations is perhaps best illustrated by the feelings, attitudes, and opinions that the civilians, including Dr. Karadzic, had for former JNA officers. The former JNA officers were not pro-Serb nationalists. The new political wave and the new political party seeking, as the Prosecution alleges, a different makeup of Bosnia or Serbia or former Yugoslavia were indeed these pro-nationalists. Mr. Beara was politically, diametrically opposed to the politics that were being brewed in the area at that time. We have a witness and witnesses to help further establish that for the Court. For example, Dr. Srdja Trifkovic who the Prosecution seems to suggest, informally and maybe even formally, that he may not be relevant. Here is also another American journalist of Serbian descent who is an advisor to Dr. Karadzic not only in 1992 and 1993. He was at -- in Pale ^ in July of 1995. He was with Dr. Karadzic and the other civilian power brokers who were discussing and examining the facts as they unfolded in the territory. This also is quite candidly confirmed and corroborated by the witness whose diary we cited in the beginning of our discussion here today. He writes that he also met Dr. Srdja Trifkovic in Pale, that he discussed with them and they know each other obviously from before because they are both journalists. I think Dr. Srdja Trifkovic and I believe expect and believe that his testimony will enlighten us as to how diametrically opposed the civilian pro-Serb nationalists were when it came to specifically JNA staff security officers. There was not just, as I've mentioned, a dislike or displeasure. There was strong animosity and a strong distrust. We raise this point, and although this issue is on appeal, because the Prosecution admitted evidence of a deceased individual without giving us the opportunity to cross-examine him and the Court, with all due respect, granted the evidence of a Miroslav Deronjic who as we know was a civilian within Bratunac in 1992 through 1995. It's incredible to suggest that Dr. Karadzic being so diametrically opposed politically having not only animosity but, indeed, hatred for security staff officers that he would entrust and convey a secret message purportedly to kill Bosnian Muslim men in the Srebrenica area. It's not only illogical; it's unreasonable, and there is no basis for it whatsoever despite the Prosecution's attempt to give that testimony to the Court through the deceased Mr. Deronjic. On the other hand, we know that the civilian Mr. Deronjic was very close to Dr. Karadzic. On that same notion, we find it incredible that indeed Mr. Karadzic or Dr. Karadzic would have used an intermediary although he had direct access to Mr. Deronjic could have conveyed any such message if indeed that message was ever conveyed. We suggest that it was not, but just the inferences the Prosecution is trying to suggest to this Court and the way in which they speculate as to how things unfolded just do not have a sound basis in any of the facts or in logic. Other witnesses such as Dr. Srdja Trifkovic that we expect to call will also further establish that there was this great hatred and animosity by the civilians, not only at the national level through Dr. Karadzic but also at the local level in Bratunac through Mr. Deronjic. Going back a little bit to the whereabouts of Mr. Beara, some of us may be thinking, what about the witnesses that the Prosecution called and tried to lead evidence in that seemed to suggest, supposedly, that Mr. Beara was at a site where killings were being either about to happen or were already completed? We bring forth two specific categories of witnesses in this regard. First, we bring to this Court an expert witness, a psychologist here from the Netherlands who has, in my view and I think the view in all of us in this courtroom, an excellent reputation. He is an expert who will share with us, and his name is Professor Vodned [phoen]. He is an expert who will testify, and I think the issues are relevant, to the purported whereabouts of Mr. Beara, and he will specifically address those witnesses that erroneously claim they saw someone or described someone that the Prosecution is alleging is Mr. Beara. At the end of the day, he will address with us through direct examination the flaws and weaknesses of such purported identification, premised on both recognition and identification. These two, although simple concepts, are quite distinct. One is do you recognise someone you have met before, and the other category is identifying someone for the first time. We believe that through our cross-examination we've raised enough doubt that those witnesses were incorrect and erroneous, that that was Mr. Beara who they came claimed or who the Prosecution claims they have seen. Further, with Mr. Wagner, we believe that he will not only discuss how and why these witnesses are unreliable by looking at certain indicia of suspicion. He will also share with us the flaws caused and the failures committed by the Office of the Prosecution during its investigation by failing or refusing to properly conduct and show these witnesses a relatively simple and straightforward objective photo board, as it's called, which is a group of pictures, as I'm sure we all know, of people who look similar or have similar characteristics. This photo board is actually a very, very important issue for both Professor Vodned and it should be in this case. If the Prosecution want to stand by those witnesses, we must ask ourselves why didn't they use a photo board? We will hear from Professor Vodned that it is a very inexpensive and simple procedure and that any investigator in the smallest of towns is familiar with it. But in this case, what is unique and special is that the Prosecution did use a photo board in this case. The Prosecution knows how to use a photo board. The Prosecution selectively chose not to use a photo board in this case, but in two instances they tried to do it; and, my apologies to Mr. Popovic and his counsel, one was of Mr. Popovic with the testimony of a witness who was an executioner at a site. They executed the Prosecution and counsel for Mr. Popovic a stipulation in that regard, and affixed to that stipulation is an eight-man photo board of eight similarly looking individuals, and they asked this witness who testified here, you mentioned that it was a lieutenant-colonel and/or colonel that you saw at the site. This witness was given a photo board, and he said, no, these people on this photo do not contain the individuals -- on this photo board do not contain the individuals that I recall seeing at the site who were giving me orders to execute Bosnian Muslims. That same witness, however, was shown a prejudicial photo board of Mr. Beara. He was shown a picture with Mr. Beara in the centre, The only - and excuse me - older individual within the picture, the only individual whose rank is clearly depicted and his stripes clearly depicted on his left breast. That photo board is what Professor Vodned will tell you causes great prejudice. If that witness said that he saw a colonel or lieutenant-colonel and you show him a picture with one individual, a colonel who should be older, and if you show him a picture with that individual's stripes and rank, it should be easy to detect who the individual is. We were fortunate enough that that witness, also, as with Mr. Popovic, he rejected that photo and said this is not affirmatively the witness or the person I saw at the killing site when I was executing Bosnian Muslims. That, too, is in a stipulation that we filed, and it's before the Court. It's relevant because our expert will complete the story and show that the Prosecution had the ability but no interest to do a photo board with all, not just some, witnesses. Who was Ljubisa Beara? We've spent significant or at least some time discussing his whereabouts, and we'll get back to that for the other period. But who was he? During our evidence, we expect to show that Mr. Beara throughout his professional career and his personal life was a man who fostered and promoted multiethnic unit and tolerance. The evidence we expect to call will reveal that Mr. Beara when possible throughout his career and specifically during the most difficult times during the war in former Yugoslavia from 1992 to 1995 helped, assisted, organised, and saved a large number of Jewish citizens from the former Yugoslavia. And when we say large number, it's my personal knowledge from speaking with this particular witness that he gives credit to Mr. Beara for saving, in his words, in the first time in the history of the world that the Jews were not persecuted or killed. He believes as being the head of that commission that Mr. Beara is the individual who was not only instrumental but it would not have been accomplished without Mr. Beara's assistance. The number according to this witness was approximately 1.500 Jewish citizens that Mr. Beara helped evacuate and help safe during the 1992 to 1995 period. We have evidence and will bring forth the evidence that Mr. Beara also helped Croatians as well as Macedonians during that war. We have evidence and we expect to bring evidence to this Court, if necessary with your assistance, that Mr. Beara throughout the war also assisted and helped Bosnian Muslims. He had from time to time both subordinates and colleagues who were Bosnian Muslims. Mr. Beara did indeed save some of these individuals from remaining in an area even such as Bratunac. One witness in particular, his family was from Bratunac. Mr. Beara assisted his family and others that he did not know, meaning friends of this individual that he knew that he helped save, to leave because Mr. Deronjic and these civilians came in and we know because weave heard and seen the plea of Mr. Deronjic as to what occurred in Bratunac at that time. Mr. Beara did help save those people, he couldn't save everybody. Didn't save anyone and by no question and never alleged he was not responsible to save anyone. Or everyone. We expect to present evidence that Mr. Beara did not and could not have the specific intent necessary for the crimes that are alleged against him. I will address that a little later, time permitting. My learned friend asked a question, was in there a conspiracy then against Mr. Beara? Very, very difficult and complicated to prove. It is not our burden to prove whether there was a conspiracy. We bring forth the facts. But let me share with you one fact in particular, and that's a proofing note on the 23rd of October 2007. And I believe it may have an ERN number -- I mean, a 65 ter number. I was unable to find it but I do have the ERN number and I'll just share with the Court so the record is complete. That is ERN number 0624-2637. We think that examining that issue will shed further light as to how, when and why certain individuals like Deronjic and Dragan Mirkovic and others in the Bratunac area who were civilians had lied and fabricated evidence and stories. No doubt they had a motive. Crimes occurred before their very eyes, both in 1992 and in 1993. This document that I referenced and proofing note of the 23rd of October 2007 is also of a former local individual from that area. He was convicted and he pled guilty, but when he was proved and it was evidence that the Prosecution sought to leave, my learned friend Julian Nicholls, who I'm sorry he is not here and I apologise for referencing him because he is not here, he conducted that interview. And with all due respect to him, I think he certainly has the qualities -- or was a Defence attorney or has the qualities to be one. He records honestly in that proofing statement portions of that discussion with Mr. Nikolic. First he tells us that the witness stated that he learned through information that, among others, Dragomir Vasic, Miodrag Josipovic and Dragan Mirkovic held a meeting at the Bratunac MUP headquarters after the killing. I don't think we are argument about this. This is discussing after the Kravica killing. Never mentions Mr. Beara. Mr. Beara was not there, did not participate in any such crimes that occurred there. Point 2 from the 23rd of October 2007 proofing note, same document, Mr. Nicholls records that this witness also stated that: "Beara had nothing to do with the burial of the bodies at Glogova." Point 3, same document, Mr. Nicholls records that this witness

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The civilian authorities in Bratunac did not know Ljubisa Beara. Even those who claim that they met him during those events supposedly for several minutes or moments while they were conducting the transfer of detainees never before met him or had an encounter with him or under any circumstances would not have accepted or discussed any of the matters that the Prosecution has alleged that have occurred as it relates to Mr. Beara. They had their local military officers who they placed in power in that community. Military men they knew, military men that they supported and military men perhaps whom they conspired with. The Bratunac civilian authorities did not need any outside influence to assist them in the transportation of civilians or Bosnian Muslims in 1995. Their strong fisted or iron fisted power and authority by specifically Deronjic in Bratunac shows us that they did this very thing in 1992 and 1993. They were lost, the civilians in Bratunac, and were unaware how they should handle POWs. They were confused as to which sites can be utilized to hold and detain these individuals in 1995? Hardly, given that they experienced this very same thing, unfortunately, two or three years earlier. They needed no assistance, no consultation, coordination or facilitation to detain these Bosnian Muslims from Ljubisa Beara. It is, indeed, we suggest a conspiracy and we will bring forth evidence of individuals who will help further define those civilians, specifically Mr. Deronjic. We also will bring a Muslim witness, we hope, who will share with us what his views were of Mr. Deronjic, but not from a civilian perspective, but from a military perspective. This young man was in the JNA and he knew how Deronjic or what Deronjic felt about JNA officers. How he treated them and how he felt, Deronjic that is, was above both the military and the law. Interestingly, the Prosecution in its indictment also mentioned a relative, although I'm not sure if it's a first cousin, I think Nenad Deronjic, who committed crimes during this area in the Bratunac vicinity. Of course he did. Any relative, friend or family member of that power structure there had the green light to commit that because Deronjic was a strong-fisted power broker and allowed it to happen. Genocide. As with all the other counts in the indictment including extermination, persecution, murder, et cetera, the OTP again alleges that Mr. Beara organised, coordinated and facilitated the detention, transportation and summary execution of these Bosnian Muslim men. I suggest to the Court that they never answered the most simple and straightforward question. If you are going to make a claim that we've organised it, coordinated and facilitated it, inform us by whom were you so given such an order. When? Where? What was said to whom? They, during our 98 bis submissions, claimed that there was this order. They have no details to that claim. It's merely a speculative claim that Mladic passed an order to Mr. Beara. When? What was said? They are going to argue, well, certainly those types of things are not recorded. Certainly we've seen from witnesses in evidence such as Mr. Vasic, he plainly writes: "Killing. Killings are occurring and we are structuring it and we are assisting in it," in his July 1995 report. Their expert witness said that word "killing," "killings," doesn't mean really killings. It means something totally different. I suggest that the Prosecution is selective in their prosecution and I believe the evidence will help assist us in revealing that. You must also be wondering, but what about the intercepts. The intercepts seem to suggest, according to the Prosecution, that there was only one man called Ljubisa, one man who has a nickname or is called Ljubo at that time. We are presenting evidence to help define who Ljubisa Beara was by presenting evidence of people who knew him before, during and after the July 1995 period, and will confirm that indeed Mr. Beara had a rather distinct dialect formed from the Herzegovina and Croatia influences. One witness is an expert witness, Dr. Remetic. He is a linguist but also a specialist in dialects. He will help us and I believe will opine that after he read and analysed the intercepts, after he met and evaluated Mr. Beara's speech pattern and current dialect and distinct speech, that the intercepts which merely mention Ljubo, or a derivative of that, without compromise to the identity, meaning it does not say that it was Ljubisa Beara on the other line, cannot and should not be attributed to Mr. Beara. Furthermore, Dr. and Professor Remetic will address the use of the term "triage" and how it has multiple meanings and in fact does exist, despite what the Prosecution seems to suggest, in the military lexicon. We believe that evidence is critical and important because you've heard from the intercept operators. And despite our attempts at cross-examination with them to show that they have added or changed and in sometimes, in our view, respectfully, manipulated those logbooks and intercept books, those intercept operators clearly said we took down things verbatim. If someone spoke in a different dialect, we would record it and we wouldn't record it any other way. There's no evidence in those intercepts that that was the dialect that Mr. Beara uses now, used then and used his entire life. Those speech patterns cannot be changed or altered. Those intercept operators should have and would have quite candidly, wrote down the dialect Mr. Beara uses and used if he was the person who was involved in the intercept conversation. He was not and therefore you do not see that anywhere throughout the intercept documentation that is been brought forth. We do also have additional witnesses in connection with the intercept. Specifically an individual who will talk about how the wiring -- and I'm just not certain if he is going to ask for protective measures so -- I believe that he may. He is going to show us how someone can call from a third place and get connected to Badem who will then switch him and have a conversation with Zlatar. So this person calling from, let's say, Belgrade, calls Badem and Badem connects him with the individuals at Zlatar. The way the Prosecution sets their case, they put the person in Belgrade, they place them at Badem and say, He was there because he has a conversation with Zlatar and Zlatar is calling the Badem IKM or command. Untrue. That's not the way the communication system worked at that time nor how it worked at any time. This witness will help flush out those issues for us and we expect that his testimony will be quite relevant and will be rather revealing. Finally, on issues of genocide, extermination, persecution. Recently in the appellate court in the Naser Oric case rendered its judgement. In that case, the Honourable Justice Schomburg had what I felt was a quite interesting quote from Sir Isaac Isaacs -- and it is Sir Isaac Issacs, I actually checked it twice. I don't know verbatim but it really challenges Your Honours and us all to say that we can and should re-evaluate legal and factual issues and it's our opportunity to do so here. It's our duty to do that. We do not, and suggest that you won't, but to simply argue that genocide was found in the Krstic case or in the Blagojevic case is not sufficient. I think in those cases, with all due respect to them, the evidence that we've evaluated was in far greater detail, I think the evidence in those cases did not examine the anthropology or the archeology or the pathology significance of these issues and we invite the Court to look at that, as I'm sure you have, and respectfully I'm suggesting it, let's not persistently use precedents as a way to suggest that we are correct. Let's re-evaluate the facts and the law and to determine, regardless of what those decisions said, whether or not there was indeed genocide that was committed here. We suggest with the highest of respect to the victims and to the families and to the people of Bosnia, that there was no genocide. There were tragic and horrific crimes that occurred. But there was no genocide in our view. We will present evidence and one, I believe, although the Court hasn't ruled but it has not drawn an objection from the Prosecution through 92 bis, and that is the evidence of Dr. Chester Moore, an anthropologist. We also will call a forensic anthropologist to the stand, hopefully next week, Dr. Debra Komar from Albuquerque, New Mexico. We believe that both, and specifically Dr. Komar, will address and discuss with this Court the notion of minimum number of individuals as referred to here "MNI." She will also address some of the more salient and significant points where she believes that the anthropologist and archeologists that the OTP called failed in their duty to properly maintain, record and secure data and or relevant findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've still got time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wasn't sure, Your Honour. I saw you looking at me and -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why shouldn't I be looking at you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it frightens me at times. But Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't know if you were giving me a signal, so that's my only concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Finally, coupled with our evidence that we were going to bring in our case, and he was a joint witness and my learned esteemed colleague Mr. Zivanovic brought him, when we look at that anthropologist evidence from Dr. Komar and Dr. Moore, and we also take into consideration Dr. Dusan Dunjic's evidence, which is our evidence, as well, we can see that very important points, I believe, or at least we tried to make those points, and Dr. Dunjic tried to explain it during his testimony when he tried to convey to the Court, I believe that if you are going to determine or render an opinion with respect to manner of death, you must in all instances know what the cause of death was. In no instance can you conclude what the manner of death is, homicide, if you not know what the cause of death is. Dr. Dunjic as other experts used this sample methodology, and he picked out several - I think it was 50, 52 - examples of autopsy reports to suggest that it is not plausible, not reliable that one can conclude a criminal act such as homicide occurred when they identify it under the category "manner of death" when in fact under cause of death the pathologist would write "unknown" or "undetermined." If you don't know how someone died, you certainly don't know why he died, whether it was a killing or by any other means. This sample methodology Dr. Dunjic used revealed that in far too many instances we had this undetermined cause of death and that unrealistically homicide was identified as the manner of death. In any event, we expect to thoroughly analyse these autopsy reports in order to further establish that many thousands died during what Richard Butler himself coined and identified "legitimate military combat engagements." It is striking that in the autopsy reports the OTP experts find no combat engagement or no legitimate military combat engagement death. Not one person. We believe just that very fact causes not only suspicion but renders their forensic pathologist and anthropologist expert reports and opinions to be rendered unreliable. Further, I have been personally in contact with several Bosnian Muslims who were victims of crimes during the 1992 period. Although difficult, I expect and hope that they continue to have the courage to speak with me and that they can honestly recollect for this Trial Chamber consistent with the statements that they gave authorities when they were they -- ultimately they reached Tuzla, consistent with the statements that they gave the Office of the Prosecution at times when they were interviewed. They've defined and described for us that hundreds, thousands were killed in these legitimate military combat engagements. Further and perhaps finally on the issue of genocide, the honourable Alan Dershowitz in discussing the holocaust that occurred in Nazi Germany, describes genocide, and he is an esteemed colleague of ours because he practices before this Tribunal. He describes the word "genocide" and says, there's no doubt that it happened in Germany by the Nazis. However, he says that the view that genocide occurred in Srebrenica is negated by the very evacuation, removal, or deportation, legal or illegal, of the women, children, and elderly men. His suggestion is, and we believe that in order for there to have been genocide or any genocidal intent, "The children had to be killed first because they were the genetic future. They are the genes." In this case, it is, we think, extremely significant that during the evacuation process in Potocari, Srebrenica, as well as in Zepa, the children, women, and men were indeed evacuated. We believe it was a result of military necessity. We believe it was military necessity because no one knew whether there was going to be resistance to the VRS during that time period. The VRS didn't even know what the reaction would be of the Bosnian Muslim military. They were quite surprised as we've seen from videos that there was no resistance. In fact, on the 11th, perhaps planned on the 10th, the Bosnian army of the 28th Division went to the woods in Susnjari. These are significant matters. The VRS had no knowledge that there would be no resistance. If there was any attempt or any suggestion of this genocidal intent, I believe that you will find just from those facts that genocide did not occur and that at the very least Mr. Beara did not have genocidal intent, not only because of his absence or lack of presence in the area, given his complete and consistent professional attempts to try to save people of all ethnic backgrounds, that he did not participate or knew of such intent if it existed; and quite honestly, I suggest that it did not. Finally, I'm sure the Prosecution wants to discuss the logbooks, another piece of evidence that they seem to claim and have weaved into this -- its corroborative type of evidence. It's not corroborative. We will bring evidence to show this Court, again, through expert and fact witnesses to show the Court not only that there was a manipulation and an alteration of these medical records -- sorry, of these logbooks, but that in fact there's great inconsistency if we look beyond just the dates highlighted by the Prosecution. One of our experts in this case is the esteemed Professor Gogic. He is still in the process of examining and reviewing that. We have his preliminary report on this data, And we hope that when is he lists out for us what the indicia or factors of suspicion are, and I think we as reasonable people can know that some of the factors are control and custody of the logbook. If it's maintained in a proper custodial fashion, you are not as suspicious. If one individual holds it, moves it, opens it, reviews it, pulls out pages from it, of course you should be suspicious. The next indicia of suspicion is did anyone admit or can we see evidence of post facto additions, even simple dates. Did anyone open the book and insert anything in the book? If they did, even in one instance, we suspect the document. The Prosecution nonetheless says we admit that these dates were added, but that's all we are going to admit to here. These indicia of suspicion and things such as placement of entries, obliterated pages, ink colours, are important, I think, for the Court to read if you are going to rely at all on these logbooks. We think that the evidence, and I hope to call - because I've personally met with some witnesses that I am being challenged with now; I am having some difficulty, but I think it's important for the Court to hear it - that in intercepts and in logbooks people were adding individual's names in order to shift blame and responsibility. That's not a defence, and it's not our defence to suggest that others are culpable or to suggest that an empty chair may be responsible for the crimes that occurred as they suggested in the Krstic or Blagojevic case when it relates to Mr. Beara. That is not a defence. It never has been, and I'm sure it won't pass muster here. Finally, I want to discuss, if I may, pressure, pressure towards an accused, pressure from the Prosecution, pressure even from his own lawyers to give the OTP something, anything, so that they may finalise the plea negotiations that were being discussed. We have a very, very scared confidential witness who was present during the time that some of these negotiations were being undertaken between the Prosecution and an

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We hope that in the interests of justice that that confidential witness will come forth as he promised he would and will share with the Court how the Prosecution conducted these plea agreements or that plea agreement, how the Prosecution asked after years and months of this witness not mentioning Mr. Beara, all of a sudden when there was something, consideration on the table, and pleas from the Prosecution with fists slamming on the desk, pressure from his own counsel, this individual ultimately suggests and supposedly offers that, again, others were responsible. He acknowledges his culpability, not sufficiently in our view, but he also in spreading his web of lies also tries to encapsulate and include Mr. Beara. It will be difficult, and I know this, to bring this witness here. He said he'd come. He is very, very afraid. He is an honest man. He is a lawyer. He is a person who has worked at this Tribunal for some time. We think that it is important for this Tribunal to get the entire picture. Thank you. Your Honours and Mr. President, we expect that through this evidence, although I highlighted some, not all of the evidence that we hope to bring forth, that you will respectfully find that indeed there is reasonable doubt on all the charges against Ljubisa Beara and that the OTP has failed to meet its burden of proof as mandated. Thank you very much once again for the opportunity to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break now of 30 minutes because I have a meeting, and we'll start with the first witness immediately after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are most welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm the presiding judge. My name is Agius. My colleague to my immediate right is Judge Kwon; then there's Judge Stole, and to my left I have Judge Prost. This is the case against Popovic and others. You've been summoned here to give evidence by the defence team for Colonel Beara, Ljubisa Beara, And you are the very first witness. Before you start giving evidence, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration to the effect that the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth and the whole truth. The text has just been handed to you now. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I read it, it's Mr. Nikolic from the Beara Defence team who will be examining you first, And then he will be followed on cross-examination by some others presumably. Mr. Nikolic, if you could also introduce yourself to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the microphone doesn't seem to work, if we could have a little assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can try the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This one doesn't work either, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard a microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mine is on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Switch his off, please, and let him switch his on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the assistance. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alacov, I want to introduce myself. My name is Predrag Nikolic, attorney at law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel's microphone is off again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, in order not to lose time, would you mind exchanging places with him, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at all, but my microphone doesn't work either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yours is not working either now. And -- oh, none of them? Only mine, I mean, that I can understand. And I have no daughter to impress today, but will you try again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't help you from here. I mean, mine seems to be working fine, but ... Even my colleague's is not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it seems that when the witness's microphone is on it deactivates our microphones. At least, that's what it seems to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. Yeah, yeah, but it's on now. Can we work with one microphone with the witness? All right, then. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems we have dealt with the difficulty. I will introduce myself again. Predrag Nikolic, attorney at law, from Ljubisa Beara Defence team. Good morning. It seems that the microphone is working now and we can continue. Could you please introduce yourself for the record by saying your first and last name as well as the date of birth and place of birth. You don't need to stand up.

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: My name is Spiridon Alacov. I was born in 1943 on the 20th of January, 1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Tell me briefly what your educational background is.

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: I was born in Ohrid. I completed my elementary and secondary school in the field of economic affairs. After that, I enrolled at the military academy in Belgrade in 1962. I completed the ground forces academy in 1965, after which I was sent to my first garrison, which was in Raska, between Kraljevo, and Mitrovica. I spent a year there at the position of the platoon commander within an infantry company, after which I was transferred because of the needs of the service to the officer platoon of the guard's brigade in Belgrade providing direct security for the then President Tito. I was there until 1970 when I was transferred to the Benkovac Garrison. To clarify, that is between Knin and Zadar and Dalmatia. I was platoon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- company commander until 1972 when I was transferred to the garrison of Lastovo the island of Lastovo. My duty there is was security organ at the naval barracks. I was there until 1976 in late August. From there, I was sent to Belgrade to attend the staff -- command staff academy. After having completed that academy in 1976, I was transferred to the garrison of Split. I was the desk officer within the counterintelligence group of the naval military district. I remained at that post until 1983 or 4. I was then transferred to the security department of the command of the naval district as the desk officer for security. I was there until August 1988, and due to the needs of service, I was sent to the garrison of Knin. I was the chief of the security organ of the 9th corps, also known as the Knin corps. I remained in that position until late August or mid-August 1990, whereupon I returned to Split to the establishment post of assistant chief of the security department of the military naval district in charge of staff security affairs. I remained there until the end of my professional military career, which was by late June 2000. In the meantime, because of the well known events in the former Yugoslavia, I left Split together with my command for Kumbor, and I retired from there. That was my career briefly put.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your answer, you mentioned several locations of your service: Lastovo, Split, Knin, and Kumbor. Did all these locations fall in the area of the naval military district of Split?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes, all of those garrisons were under direct command of the naval military district headquartered in Split.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause before answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More or less, we are synchronized, the interpreter and myself, because you've been overlapping and you are creating difficulties. Mr. Alacov, try to allow a short pause after Mr. Nikolic has finished his question in the same language you speak because the interpreters have still got to translate to us who don't understand your language. Yes, Mr. Nikolic. Sorry for having interrupted you like this, but it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alacov, to go back now to the period when you were on Lastovo, what was your position there?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: In the garrison of Lastovo, I was the security desk officer at the naval military garrison barracks there. It was the first post I had in the field of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Mr. Beara, and if so, on what occasion?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after my arrival in Lastovo, a few months after that, perhaps two or three months later, Mr. Ljubisa Beara, together with a team from the counterintelligence group, officially visited Lastovo attending to some tasks assigned to him by his superiors. Upon his arrival in Lastovo, Mr. Ljubisa Beara introduced himself and explained that he was there to attend to some business that needed to be done in that territory. He introduced himself and then his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Judging by your answer, you were at the time working for the security service. Was that closely related with the counterintelligence group?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes, the spheres of activity overlap as well as the competences of the counterintelligence group and our garrison. It had to do with the army units. My competence was the unit I worked in. I was in charge of its internal security. However, the jobs are almost identical, and they overlap in many segments of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was that overlap the reason why you met Mr. Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes. It is customary when one goes to an area covered by a certain security organ that that person from the outside should introduce themselves. Mr. Ljubisa did so not only for the official reasons, but he seemed to be very pleasant. He introduced himself, and we spent time together during the period that he was there. It was only a few days, but we also saw each other outside working hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alacov, and last of all, you were still a young man, relatively young for someone involved in security activities. What impression did you gain after having met these counterintelligence officers, in particular Mr. Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: By that time, I had only begun working for the security service, and that contact meant a lot to me, particularly because on the island of Lastovo there were no other security organ members. And I don't know how familiar you are with that, but Lastovo is a remote island, and travel and communication via telephone was made difficult. I made the best use of that meeting, and Mr. Ljubisa was very open, and he was kind enough to explain to me some things that pertained security, what one needs to do, focus on, and what methodology to use. Although it was not his task, he did so as an experienced member of the security organ. That situation contributed much to my knowledge in that first phase of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it was an incentive for your future work. Were you able to later in the course of your work contact and ask Mr. Ljubisa Beara's opinion on various things, regardless of whether it was directly related to your work as the security officers but maybe only because you had a question that had to do with your sphere of activity alone rather than his?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: When we met, we didn't only discuss official affairs. Ljubisa was very accessible, very open, and although it was a very brief period of time, our relationship resembled two people who have known each other for awhile. Just before he departed, he invited me to drop by their office whenever I am in Split to either have a cup of coffee together or a chat, and whenever I had time and travelled to Split, I did go to their offices in my free time, in my spare time, and contacted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From your answer, it seems that the next post you held was in Split. What was your duty there?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Having completed the command staff academy in 1978, I was transferred to the garrison of Split. My establishment post there was the desk officer of the counterintelligence group of the naval military district. In that period, the naval captain at the time, Ljubisa Beara, was no longer with the counterintelligence group. As far as I can recall, at first he was the desk officer of the security department of the command of the military naval district.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you continue your relationship not only in professional terms but also privately?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes. Along professional lines as the desk officer, he was supposed to supervise my work. We worked in the same sector, but it was then that we began spending time together privately but it lasted for a short while only. As far as I can recall, Ljubisa Beara in early 1979 was transferred to the garrison of Kumbor to work for the security organ there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On your -- or rather, on his return from Kumbor, was he at any point your superior?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes. He was my immediate superior when he took up the post of chief of the security department of the counterintelligence group. However, he had a superior role, also, while he was deputy chief of the security department, while I still held the post I had in the counterintelligence group and the desk officer in the security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alacov, your relations are now those of superior and subordinate. Can you describe to me the characteristics of Ljubisa Beara as a superior; how did he treat you and other subordinate officers?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: As a superior officer, I can say that he was very correct, always willing to help, always ready to guide, to provide guidance and to explain how things should be done. He asked that things be done well and in a timely manner. As I said, neither I nor my colleagues ever hesitated to consult him, to ask him for guidance, to ask him for advice or for instructions as to how best to do our tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, at that time in Split, what was the ethnic breakdown of the security organ you worked in?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that it was heterogenous. There were Slovenians, Muslims or Bosniaks, Croats, Macedonians. At that time, we didn't pay special attention to people's ethnic background. There was Hazim Begovic, who was a Muslim or Bosniak; there was Vjeloslav Runje, who was a Croat; Miloje Garanovic, who was either a Serb or a Macedonian, he was born in Skopje; and there were other persons, so there were people from all the parts of the former Yugoslavia, all the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now that we are talking about the ethnic makeup, let me ask you about your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: I was born in Macedonia, so according to my place of birth I am a Macedonian. My parents were Macedonian. I grew up in Macedonia and lived there for awhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that at one period you served in Knin. What post did you hold there and in what unit?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: I served in Knin from the end of August 1988 until August 1990. There I was appointed head or chief of the security organ of the 9th Corps. At that time, the 9th Corps was being established and that command was being formed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So in 1990 you returned to Split. Did you return to the same post?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I still had the same post and the same function.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let's dwell a little on the end of 1990 and the beginning of 1991. What was the security and political situation like bearing in mind that wartime tensions were already mounting in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: From the end of 1989 and even before that, ethnic tensions began mounting. Various events upset people, and nationalism began to awake on both sides. The tensions escalated to such an extent that people began to build barricades made of logs; and as the Knin area has a mixed population, there are villages with Serb populations and villages with Croat populations, people built barricades to protect themselves from one another. People organised themselves because they wanted to avoid being taken by surprise. Relations deteriorated to such an extent that this later became an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let's dwell a little on the city of Split. You yourself said that ethnic tensions grew. Your service had a heterogenous ethnic makeup, so to what extent did all this effect the work of the service? How was it reflected in the work of the service?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Generally speaking, among the members of the security organ relations were quite stable. We didn't feel the influence of these events to a large extent. Some persons would as a joke rather than anything else start putting forward their ethnic affiliation, not maliciously. Before that, we hadn't paid attention to other people's ethnic backgrounds, but now we started taking an interest in who was from where and what their ethnic affiliation was. It was then that I learned that Ljubisa Beara was a Serb and not a Croat. All the time I had thought he was a Croat because he used the Croatian dialect with a Dalmatian accent, or rather, the Croatian language and he used the Dalmatian dialect, but he continued to speak in the same way as before, not just he but others also. I can say that Ljubisa Beara and the others tried very hard to retain the unity of the service. I can tell you about an incident that happened, a colleague of ours who worked in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a little bit. We are straying from our topic, so excuse me for interrupting. We spoke about the mounting tensions in Split. What were the causes of this mounting tension, and what was the position of the JNA organ and the military naval district?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: If you are referring to the position of members of the army, of the territory military district and the overall situation, we were subject to all sorts of pressure. Certain officers -- well, they started following us, or rather, the members of the ZNG started following us around, threatening our families, denying the commands of the units supplies which were absolutely necessary, such as food, power, water; telephone lines were cut off, and this was mainly in 1990 and onwards. They harassed our families, especially those of members of the security organs and the commanding officers of the military naval district and its command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At that time, was Ljubisa Beara your superior officer?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes, he was. It was precisely then that he was chief of the security department and I was assistant chief of the security organ for staff security affairs, and I was directly subordinate to Captain Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind everything you've said, the provocations and so on, I'm interested in Ljubisa Beara's response as a superior officer who had certain responsibility for organising the service under these circumstances. Please give me some examples as to how and in what direction he made attempts to deal with this situation within his service.

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Well, both before this period and especially during this period, he insisted that all tasks be carried out in a highly professional manner in the spirit of the rules and regulations governing the work of the security organ and the armed forces of the SFRY. He did not permit any deviation from this or any improvisation. He especially insisted that we guard ourselves and our units from any unwanted consequences either with respect to other persons, especially civilians, or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What measures did he order to be taken in relation to these provocations, such as cutting off electrical power, water, and other utilities, which all, you will admit, caused nervousness among you?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: The organs of command took measures through the official authorities as far as was possible at the time and as far as this functioned at the time to avoid such things happening. From time to time, these things were dealt with and they would stop but then they would happen again. Ljubisa Beara through representatives of the ministry of the interior in Split and other institutions made efforts to have these situations resolved peacefully without the use of force or any other undesirable measures, and force was not used until the breakout of the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did this situation cause the awakening of nationalism among individuals within the command?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: As for extreme situations regarding the awakening of nationalism in the security organ, this did not happen, but people did begin to leave the service, for example, and they were allowed to do this without any obstruction. They did this quite legally. Among the first to leave was then Captain Curko Stojan. He was the first to legally leave the security organ and take up another post, and later on he left the navy. He left the JNA altogether. Among the others, I wouldn't say they were hostile, but there is an event that sticks in my mind which occurred in the office of Flag Officer Petrovic, Color Sergeant Dragan Petrovic, who was then taking care of the archives within the security organ. He was in charge of the archives, and I was there when Ljubisa Beara entered his office and color sergeant Petrovic took from his -- took from his desk a Sajkaca. This an old fashioned Serbian cap with a Chetnik symbol. He put it on his head, and he said, Ljubo, look at this. He was a non-commissioned officer but yet he addressed him as Ljubo, by his first name, because that shows how close we are. We were on first-name terms, all of us. So when Ljubisa Beara was the captain of a war ship saw this, he told him to take that cap off his head. He said that such things could not be kept on the premises of the armed forces. They couldn't be brought to the office. He told him to pack it up and take it back where it came from, and he criticized him for bringing such things on to our premises. I apologise to the interpreters, but I don't think there is any need for me to stress that the Sajkaca cap is not a nationalistic symbol per se. It's a regular traditional cap worn even nowadays in Serbia, however, without the symbol.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alacov, I'm interested in this situation and the reaction of such an officer such as Officer Ljubisa Beara in the situation where certain people were leaving the service on the one hand. On the other hand, the barracks were being blockaded; there were tensions; electricity and water supply were cut off. How did he try to deal with those things, and what instructions did he give you?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Whoever expressed their wish to leave the security organ or the armed forces of the SFRY, that was approved without any pressure or obstacles. Some people expressed their wish for the pressures they felt to move to other services of the armed forces, whereas some others stated that they wanted to leave the armed forces altogether.
