Whoever expressed such a wish, their request was met, and the Naval Captain Beara stood by the principle that the work is prescribed by the rules of service of the security organ, that such work is voluntary and that whenever somebody wants to leave, may do so. However, that person is still under the obligation to keep state and other secrets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alacov, all of us who hail from the region know of an event that took place in Split that was carried by the media. It is usually referred to as the Split Strangler incident. Can you tell us what happened, and how did the security service deal with it? Who headed the security's activities pertaining to that, and how was it all concluded?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: The propaganda that was in place at the time generally speaking and across all spheres of politics blurred everyone's vision. Some people believed all of the information that was served by various media. It culminated in early May 1992. They said it was spontaneous; however, I believe otherwise. In any case, there was a gathering in front of the naval military district command building, and it was blocked. The truth of the matter was that people were sent from their companies to go and to come in front of the building and demonstrate against what they termed the Serbian army, although at the time we were still the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Why was that incident characteristic? Why was it called the Split Strangler?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: It is a well known incident because certain extremist groups among the mass of people there tried to create chaos. It was clear that they were seeking to provoke the use of force. The incident is well known because the first soldier of the JNA was killed by the name of Gesovski of Macedonia. He was a sentry and did nothing to cause fire being opened at him. It is also known for certain extremist groups which acted violently against the security forces. A group of them mounted an armoured vehicle, an armoured personnel carrier, that was there to provide security for the command. There was a very strong young man who grabbed a soldier whose head was protruding through an opening of the armoured carrier, trying to pull him out of the vehicle by the neck. We were instructed strictly to avoid any use of force. We could have used ammunition and explosives, but there were masses of people there, and had something like that happened, there would have been many more innocent victims except for the strangler. He was called the strangler because he grabbed the soldier by the throat trying to pull him out and nearly killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said that you were instructed not to use mines and weapons. Who issued that order?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: The command. I know that the naval captain had a role in that. He himself suggested that force be not used, and when assigning tasks he would regularly instruct us that we should resort to arms only if strictly necessary, as the last resort in trying to save our lives. He suggested to the command that an order be issued prohibiting the use of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We can see that there was a lot of provocation, that a soldier was hurt. Did the security service try to identify the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Just another thing concerning the event before I answer. When the command of the naval military district was blocked by the citizens, some extremist groups also blocked the movement of a column of armoured personnel carriers, which were on their way to the naval military district command to provide additional security. That part of the unit was stopped along the road by an extremist group. A crew was kicked out of an armoured vehicle, and it was taken away, the vehicle, that is. By constant talks and negotiations over the phone with MUP representatives, the naval Captain Beara managed to have the armoured carriers brought back and secured by our personnel. Later on, they were indeed returned to the unit they had been taken from. Therefore, there was no use of force or weapons, and it was done in that way. Sorry, your question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let's take it slowly. Answer this first, please: How do you know that it was Ljubisa Beara himself that contacted and talked on the phone with the MUP representatives?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Since it was practically a state of emergency, we were constantly in our offices in a state of ready, and I was in the office at the moment when he spoke on the phone. I was with the naval captain Beara. There were several such conversations that took place to deal with other cases, as well, but this was the one I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To go back to one of my previous questions, I don't think you've answered that, did the security service take any measures in order to capture the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes. Since there was a lot of damage and a human life was lost and among other things, it also constituted an attack on a legally formed armed forces in Croatia. We tried contacting the MUP, without much hope, though, but the security administration insisted that we take measures to identify the main players, in particular, the killer of the soldier and the strangler's identity as well as the identity of the remaining three persons. I cannot recall their names off the cuff. A lot of time has passed. We were assigned the task from the security administration as well as their assistance in dealing with that issue. With that goal in mind, the then chief of the security administration, General Aco Vasiljevic arrived at the naval district. He issued instructions and helped us to deal with the situation. In a short span of time, we managed to identify those people and to apprehend them and detain them in the military prison. Later on, they were interrogated and taken over by the court. I know that finally they were exchanged. Excuse me, we did not manage to apprehend the person who opened fire killing the soldier, but according to our information that person enjoyed the protection of the organs of the MUP of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alacov, did Mr. Ljubisa Beara take part in that operation, and if so, what was his role?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes. As head of the security department, he was the person in charge of the operation. We drew up a plan of action. We assigned people and went through a process of preparation with them. He also managed the operation until its completion. It was done, I should say, without any use of weapons or any beatings or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Obviously, the operation and the incident was at the peak of the tensions. In your sector, that is, the security organ, what was the ethnic makeup at the time? Was it still mixed?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes. A few people had left by the time, such as Crnko, that I mentioned, later on Zoran Radic left as well. There were a few others who left, but in total there weren't many of them, and the makeup was still heterogenous, and it remained so even up until the time that we were relocated to Kumbor. I may be more specific if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Take it slowly, please. In the course of your answer, you managed that Ljubisa had a particular accent and that you thought him to be Croatian for that. However, now you know that he is a Serb, and at the time of that operation you knew that as well. In the course of such tensions, did he ever act inappropriately or did he present himself as a nationalist?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: I never noticed anything of the sort. He continued behaving and speaking in the same fashion. At no moment did I see that he had any bias, that he held anything against people of other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that the naval military district command was relocated to Kumbor. Why did it take place and when?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: After the May events and contrary to the promises made by the authorities that the tension would be reduced and problems resolved, the situation grew even more complex. Our electricity was being cut off as well as the water supply, food supply, and we were no longer able to use regular communication routes and modes of transport. There were other things as well. There was a danger of us being completely cut off so that we would be forced to surrender the command facilities. That is why in the course of August, a decision was made that was supposed to provide for the continuity of command, and for that reason a part of the command was supposed to be relocated to a forward command post, as we would say in the armed forces. That was supposed to take place on the island of Vis. The commander left for the island with some other members of the command. It was also foreseen that the shifts would take up to a week. However, around the 9th or 10th of September, we were indeed cut off completely and blocked, and those people who were on the island of Vis at the time remained there. I was one of those. We remained there until the moment that the entire command and units were taken outside Croatia. It was all preceded by a long-lasting process of negotiation under the auspices of many international organizations, which by that time had arrived in the territory. We negotiated with the authorities to provide for a safe pullout of the forces, their family members, and equipment from the territory of Croatia. It was towards the end of 1991, December 1991, although I cannot recall the exact date. It was then that the last unit pulled out of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alacov, we'll move on to another topic now. At the time you were serving in Split and in Knin - but let's talk about Split first - was General Tolimir serving in Split?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes, at the time he was a captain. Before that, he had served in Velas in Macedonia and he and another captain, Steta, were transferred to fill vacant posts -- vacant establishment posts in Split. I can't recall the exact years they arrived, but it was sometime around 1983. It might have been a year before or a year later, I'm not sure, but both Tolimir and Captain Steta were appointed to the establishment post of desk officers in the counterintelligence group of Split. That was the first time I encountered Tolimir, when he arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At that time, what duty was Ljubo Beara performing when Tolimir arrived in Split?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: I think it was at that time that he had returned from the Kumbor garrison, and as far as I can recall he was appointed assistant chief of the counterintelligence service of the Split naval military district, or rather, chief of the security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At that time, was Beara superior to Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: No. He was not his direct superior officer. The chief of the counterintelligence group was his immediate superior, and he was subordinate to the chief of the counterintelligence group, but there were contacts and exchange of information and experience, provision of instructions, but only as regards professional matters, the technical aspects of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So at that time you were there -- so can you tell us what the relationship was between Beara and Tolimir? Were they merely acquainted as officers, and what was their professional relationship?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Well, if you want to talk about their personal relationship, I just mentioned that Ljubisa was a very open, accessible, friendly person. As we had spent a long time there and socialized for a long time, I knew that, but as far as I know he didn't socialize with Tolimir especially. Their contacts were purely professional as far as I know. They didn't visit each other's homes to the best of my knowledge, and at that time there was already a circle of friends who knew each other from before whom he socialized with, so as far as I know they didn't have any private social contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As you were in Split until the dislocation of the military naval district, at that time was Tolimir in Split the whole time?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Tolimir was in Split and held the same establishment post until August 1990, except for the period when he went for further training. In August 1990, he came to the Kumbor garrison to replace me at my establishment post, and I returned to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said that he came to your place in Kumbor, to your post in --

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: No, in Knin, sorry. It was in Knin that he took up the establishment post of chief of the security organ of the command of the 9th Corps, and he replaced me at that post. I do apologise if I said Kumbor. I meant Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you had been in Knin up to that point?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes, from 1988 until August 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who at the time was the commander of the 9th Corps known as the Knin corps?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: The commander of the 9th corps was General Trajcevski, Tomislav Trajcevski, who arrived from the command of the then 3rd Army in Skoplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The 9th corps or the Knin corps as it was called, was it part of the military naval district of Split?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes. The 9th corps was directly subordinate to the command of the military naval district in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I see that you mentioned in that period. Was there another period when it was not part of the military naval district?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: When the armed conflict started and towards the end of 1991, the 9th corps was subordinate to the General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY along one chain of command. It was in the rear of the command of a military naval district, and in operative terms part of it was under the command of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alacov, please tell me, in that period at any point was General Mladic the commander of this corps?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: While I was the -- while I was serving in Knin, Mladic did not hold any position in the 9th Corps. When I left in August 1990 and when Tolimir arrived, Spiro Nikovic, General Spiro Nikovic was appointed commander, but he didn't stay there long. Perhaps a year. I didn't see Mladic, but I heard that he came to Knin, but this was certainly after June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Although you assume that General Mladic arrived and took up the corps commander only in June 1991, the military naval district and you as officers and the security organs and Ljubisa Beara as the chief of that organ remained in Split for a certain time because you said that in late 1991, you were dislocated. Do you know whether in that period Mr. Beara and General Mladic had either private or official contacts?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Let me tell you that for a while Mladic was Chief of Staff, and after Nikovic left he took up the duty of commander. And let me also tell you that in view of the situation at the time, it was very difficult to move around and communicate, and there was very little time, or rather, no time for any personal contacts and for socializing. I have no information or knowledge that Beara ever socialized with Mladic. It's possible that there were brief professional official contacts when they both went to briefings at our command while it was still possible or in the course of brief visits by the security organ, Beara to Knin. But this may have amounted to two or three visits in that period to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Answering my questions, you said that General Tolimir moved from Split to Knin in 1990 if I remember correctly. Please tell me, to the best of your knowledge did he go back to Split or did he remain in the Knin corps?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: After the dislocation of the units of the military naval district from the territory of Croatia, the 9th corps remained for awhile on the territory it was responsible for so that Tolimir also remained with that unit. But I don't know until when because after we left, I lost contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So the military naval district had a new headquarters, a new area; can you tell us where this was?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: That was the Kumbor garrison in the Montenegrin coastal area. Herceg Novi was the first -- the nearest larger town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before you, there were huge tasks. You had to find headquarters for the command. Who coordinated this work on behalf of your service, and did you have any cooperation with the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: If you are referring to Montenegro, on the territory of Montenegro, yes, we did have direct cooperation, and certain civilian facilities were given over to our use for the accommodation of our units and commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Colonel Beara was in the administration in Kumbor at the time. Did he organise the work of the service?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes. Persons, or rather, members of security organs from all the units were there in a small area. We were overstaffed, and in view of the new needs and circumstances, a new establishment structure had to be put in place and appointments made, or rather, the establishment post had to be filled, and administratively the status of all these persons had to be dealt with and Captain Beara was in charge of all this. He proposed certain solutions to the command of what was by then the navy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From your testimony today, it follows that you spent quite a long period of time either serving with or close to Beara from the beginnings of your work in Lastovo until Kumbor where you were from, or rather, this is the period from 1973 to 1991. And when did you part ways, you and Colonel Beara finally?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Well, we never did, but we did say farewell in July 1992 when he left to take up another establishment post. I think it was for awhile in the security administration and then I don't know; he went to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, this was a long time ago, 1992, but I see that you knew each other well, that you were friends, as you say. Can you describe Ljubisa Beara to me as he was in 1992 when you saw him for the last time? What is the image that sticks in your mind? What did he look like physically?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Well, I'll take the liberty of saying that as for three or four months we had been separated, he was in Split and I was on Vis. Our first encounter was in Kumbor after August 1991, and our next meeting was in late January 1992. He looked as he usually did but was a little thinner. He is a tall man. If I have to describe him physically, he had sideburns. He wore glasses. He looked after his appearance. He was neat and tidy, always clean shaven, always appropriately dressed. His clothes were always clean and ironed. I especially remember his shoes because they were always very shiny, as if they were patent leather shoes. That's how shiny they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Alacov. Evidently, Ljubisa Beara is a man you remember as a good man. Were you ever in a situation including these dramatic times in Split ever to observe or sense or feel that Ljubisa Beara took up a nationalist stance in relation to anybody, not just professionally but in your private socializing?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: In relation to me, there was never a gesture, never a statement where he ever expressed any sort of nationalist sentiment. He never offended me in any way, and I never observed him acting in that way towards anybody else either. On the contrary, in that very sensitive situation he never paid attention to people's ethnic background, to people's religious affiliation, but when appointing people to establishment posts, all he cared about was people's qualifications and the quality of their work. In those critical years when nationalism was burgeoning and negative tensions were mounting, he appointed Major Tole Zarko as battalion commander, for example. I also know that in that critical period, he helped while I was in Knin my subordinate captain Peter Jukic to be from Knin to Split and to be appointed -- and he was a Croat by ethnicity, and he was appointed to the establishment post of the security organ in the protection regiment. This protection regiment was a very important unit. After the dislocation to Kumbor, the then-lieutenant commander Ramiz Dugalic who was a Muslim was appointed deputy chief of the counterintelligence group, so there are other examples to demonstrate that he did not have any prejudices against people of different ethnic affiliations. Although I am a Macedonian, I remained at the establishment post I held before, and this was a leading position in the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alacov, for your exhaustive replies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I didn't interrupt you before as we were approaching the break time because I noticed you were approaching the end. I thank you, Mr. Nikolic, I thank you, Mr. -- or Colonel Alacov. We'll have a short break now of 25 minutes. And then we'll start with the cross-examinations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, do you wish to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated] Madam Nikolic, do you wish to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic has already indicated there is no cross. Correct, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No questions from the Miletic Defence team. We are not aware you would like to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I was about to apologise for the fact that we hadn't provided a filing. Apologies, anyway. It won't surprise the Trial Chamber. No, we have absolutely no questions for this witness whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sarapa, would you like to cross-examine this witness? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That brings us to you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'll have brief cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. My name is Kweku Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He's not hearing? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Alacov, you can here me now; is that right? All right. Good afternoon to you. My name is Kweku Vanderpuye, and on behalf of the Prosecution, I'm going to put some questions to you in relation to your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the very last thing that you spoke about before we broke about a half an hour ago is you indicated that you were not aware of any particular event in which Mr. Beara had offended anybody or paid any particular attention to a person's ethnic background. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the term "Turk" as is used to describe a Bosnian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: I heard of such a term. Do you mean when used in derogatory fashion? Well, I never heard that word from Captain Beara; at least, I was never present on such occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about the term "balija"? Have you heard that term?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: I did hear about that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And is that a derogatory term as well?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In fact, it's an extremely offensive and demeaning term, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Depends on one's understanding and depending on what occasion it is used. There are different offensive words in particular in the Serbian language which can have a particular weight given the context or the situation in which they are used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Is that the kind of language that you would expect a high-ranking officer in the army to use?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: If it is an official communication, in that case it would be inappropriate. If -- on the other hand, if we have two people speaking in jest or in their unofficial capacity, then it could take place especially among those of us who hail from the south. One could then hear terms of such nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, have you ever heard Mr. Beara use those terms?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: I was never present on such an occasion, and I don't remember him using such terms. Maybe even I used some terms in different situations but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, Let me acquaint you with a document that's 65 ter 539. Now, this is a document as you can see from the bottom that is type-signed Ljubisa Beara. It's dated 16th August 1995, And this is a communication; it says supreme military corps; it has a strictly confidential number 15/95. You can see right there, right in the first line where Mr. Beara is referring to all the POWs from the former balija enclave of Zepa. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you go on a little bit further on in the document, you can see right after there is a reference to the members of the VRS, on the next line it says that members of the VRS and RS Republika Srpska MUP and the security organs who will interrogate the captured balija in order to provide criminal justice documentation. Do you see that? That's right there in the second line of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: I can't see it very well, but I'll take your word for it. I trust that what you read is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you down to the third paragraph, and if you look at the last sentence of that, you can see where it says to do this to investigating judges with typists and deputy prosecutor should be sent to Serbian correctional facilities to so the criminal law? "Documentation can be formed immediately after the interrogation of the balija." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In relation to one of the last questions that was put to you, you also indicated that when it came to making appointments, that all Mr. Beara was concerned about was the qualifications and the quality of the work of the people that he was selecting. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me acquaint you with another document. Could I have 65 ter 3502 in e-court, please. All right. We don't have the English -- yeah, we do have the English. Okay. This is a document -- if we can go to the second page just for a moment so I can show the gentleman that this is a document that is signed by -- you see that it's signed by Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is a document that is dated 27th November 1995. Has a number, strictly confidential number of 12/46-701/95, and what it talks about is choosing a number of NCOs and soldiers from the military police battalion as a personal escort for members of the Main Staff. Now, if you go, if we could, if we could go to the bottom of this page in the B/C/S, and if we could go to the second page in the English. The second paragraph of the English, it reads "The NCOs and soldiers appointed for escort duty should excel in military conduct and appearance as well as in military knowledge and well-mannered behaviour in similar. They may only be Serbs and not those from mixed marriages or those whose family members live in the territory controlled by the enemy." These are among the criteria that Mr. Beara has specified are to be found or to be observed in filling this position. This relates to more than just whether or not a person is qualified, doesn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct factually speaking, and that is what it says. However, we seem to be forgetting one fact, and that is that in the period that I talked about, while the unified Yugoslavia was still in existence, that at that time there was still the army of Yugoslavia that existed. However, this period is in 1995 already when the opposing parties were Serbs and Muslims, Bosniaks. To me, it seems normal that when choosing the candidates for a post like that one bears in mind certain things. This should not be insulting to anyone, the fact that I as a Macedonian or another person who is a Bosniak would not be considered. The conditions were different; the situation was different from that when we were still together. I talked about the period before June 1992. After that, we went our separate ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think you actually said in your testimony that you never parted ways even though physically you parted. What I'd like to know is whether or not in your view the words that are written here reflect somebody's or a person's paying attention to a person's ethnicity above all in relation to filling a qualified position?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: I think that what they had in mind was to choose the persons who would fully implement the tasks they were assigned, much as you would choose your work team. On top of their abilities, you also consider who and what they are. By the same token, the other side also has the right to choose the people who are going to be assigned certain tasks. To my mind, this is no insult or disadvantage that someone may not be considered for a certain position. I should not be offended if I am not appointed as your assistant because I was not qualified, and in this particular consideration other circumstances played a role too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And That qualification can just depend on who it is you happen to have married before the conflict in your view? That's right, Mr. Alacov, isn't it? One of the criteria you see in here says "not those from mixed marriages." That's justifiable in your view, right, Mr. Alacov?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Well, the situation evidently showed that in the course of the breaking up of Yugoslavia, that some people who hailed from mixed marriages fell under the influence of their wives and other members of their family. They left the armed forces, and they abandoned the service, which they had sworn to protect, saying that they would conscientiously perform their tasks. Instead, they were under the influence of their family members and leaving the armed forces at the very moment when they were needed the most. That was the starting point. As well as based on the experience of others, this is normal. When electing persons to sensitive positions, this also had to be borne in mind. As far as I knew, this is something you find in each and every army of the world. Some people cannot be trusted with certain functions if they don't meet the other criteria. There's also a categorization of officers in terms of category 1, 2 and 3, and you know exactly to what level a certain officer can advance. It is not my fault that I would, for example, fall in category 3. I shouldn't be angry by that -- because of that. And as far as I know, such categories exist in foreign armies as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. What category would somebody like General Miletic fall into?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object. I object. I really don't see the purpose of this question. This is a witness testifying to the character of another person. He didn't even talk about the Army of Republika Srpska. We don't even know if he knows General Miletic. Maybe it would be good to start -- for a start to know whether he knows General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think he has answered the question. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination, Mr. Nikolic? Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alacov, during your military service, were you a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was one of the criteria to be accepted for military service and to obtain senior military positions, was the membership in the league a precondition?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: Well, there were some army members who were not members of the party, but they were not assigned leading positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You told that during the time you talked about your command and the armed forces reflected the multiethnic composition of the then state. My question is this: Was one of the criteria used to elect people to the senior positions in the army the ethnic key, that is to say that they hailed from a particular ethnic group which was represented the most in any -- in that given area?

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: At the beginning of my military career, there was a principle in place that to the extent possible, especially in managing positions, there should be a proportionate representation of people of different ethnic backgrounds. However, later on the principle was liberalised, relaxed, and especially for those other duties, the practice was to employ people who hailed from the area where the garrison was. However, for the senior positions, the ethnic key was still used so that there wouldn't be people of a single ethnicity occupying most of the senior positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alacov, former Yugoslavia fell apart, and for the most part national states were created. What is your opinion? Would it have been possible and logical in an elite unit such as we could see from the document supposed to provide security for the most senior officials to be elected into it if one were, say, a Serb coming from a mixed marriage living in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see that the question invites speculation in this respect. The witness is not testifying as an expert, and the questions I put to him related to the specific document that was presented to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can understand why and when you stood up because -- to object because that was after the use by counsel of what is your opinion. However, later on, actually, he is asking a very specific question, which can be answered by the witness based on his expertise. But still, I don't blame you for standing up at the time. Yes, Colonel Alacov, could you answer the question, please. It's a very simple one. Would it have been possible and logical in an elite unit such as we could see from the document supposed to provide security for the most senior officials to be elected into it if one were, say, a Serb coming from a mixed marriage living in Croatia? And What is not clear in my mind exactly is what period and time are you referring the witness to? Is it before Yugoslavia fell apart or when the war was on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had in mind the post-war period. In my previous question, I said that several nation states were formed, and my question pertained to the period after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. The period after the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Either way. During the war or after 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then you can split your answer into two parts, during the war and after the war. If you can answer the question. If you are not in a position to answer the question, please tell us so, and we'll move to the next one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to answer. At the outset, I have to say that in any event or in any rule there are exceptions. If there is information in existence about someone that that person is loyal and that accepts the basic ideology or position, then that person is included in such a unit. However, we have exceptions, but rules are not based on those. In the Serbian army today there are Serbs, members of the army, who hail from Croatia or Republika Srpska, that is, Bosnia-Herzegovina. As to whether they occupy senior positions or not, I have no knowledge of it. Well, there may be some in senior positions, but what do you define -- how do you define a senior position? The Chief of Staff of the General Staff, or as far as I know, the person occupying that position currently hails from Knin. I don't know whether I've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Alacov, there were two questions. Please pay a bit more attention to what I'm about to say now. Based on everything you've said so far, was it possible in the course of the war in an elite unit in Croatia that a person be appointed into that unit assigned to provide security for senior officials and provided that person was of Serbian origin; and the second question is whether something like that would be possible in the newly formed states after the war.

utterances.speaker: SPIRIDON ALACOV
utterances.text: To repeat what I've said, there are exceptions to any rule. In the course of the war or a war, it is difficult to get by information on people's affiliation. People often find themselves in such fluctuating situations, and one changes affiliation and behaviour frequently. There are those who represent a position today, changing it the very next day. If someone falls under the influence of another, they can change their views causing more damage than good. During the combat operations in Croatia, there were members of other ethnicities in senior positions as well. There was an Albanian who commanded a brigade. He is one of the accused before this Tribunal, Mr. Ademi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alacov.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Kwon, do you have any questions? Judge Stole? We don't have any further questions for you, Colonel, which means you are free to go. Our staff will give you all the assistance you require. On behalf of everyone, I would like to thank you for having come over and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I'd like to thank everyone who was of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no documents to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President I have 65 ter 539 and 65 ter 3502.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We object to the 1996 document because it is outside the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to respond to that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The documents I showed to the witness, Mr. President, were 1995 documents, both of them were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I think, but I'm not here to argue the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Evidently, I overlooked the date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it means that you have no objection basically. All right. Thank you, so they are both admitted. Which brings us to the next witness. Is he here? One moment. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before hearing the testimony of the next witness so that we aren't faced with any surprises, I would like to ask you for supplementary guidelines on the cross-examination led by the Prosecution because if the Prosecution is allowed to ask questions that have nothing to do with the examination-in-chief and to mention an accused that is not at all prepared, this is not fair to the Defence. I'm not asking you to completely forbid such questions, but in such a case the Prosecution should be obliged to inform the Defence counsels of the other accused who might be mentioned in the cross-examination so we can prepare adequately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can see your point, of course, and I appreciate it, but on the other hand a cross-examination is what it is. And most of the time, one doesn't anticipate or can't anticipate much. One question follows another sometimes; the next question was never intended, and it is put precisely because of the answer to the previous question. So I remember when I used to cross-examine, myself, that I would just scrap all the papers and everything that would have prepared, finding myself faced with new facts. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully agree with you; nonetheless, I find that the question regarding my client that was addressed to the witness was just completely out of the context of the cross-examination and had nothing to do with what the witness had said, could not at all have been deduced or derived from the answers of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. Do you wish to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you'd like me to, I will. I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It was directly related to the answer that the witness gave. The witness gave -- the witness precisely responded to the question of considering one's ethnicity in terms of the advancement or the possibilities that are available to a person coming from a mixed marriage, and that is precisely the reason why the question was put to the witness, and it is also exemplary, I think, of the credibility of the witness in terms of his assessment of the significance of that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you both. I'm sure that in the future if there are cases which are -- justify attracting such questions or problems, we'll deal with them as they arise, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, but that's exactly my point of view. I think that in fact now we are in a situation that is not at all fair to the witness. He answered a precise question. He said, I don't know. We have no idea whether this witness ever heard of a General Miletic, if he knows what were his functions within the army of the Republika Srpska. We do not know if he knows that General Miletic is married to a Croatia woman. We have no idea of any of that, and we know that the witness does not know to which category General Miletic belongs, so I don't see how he can assess such evidence in the context or given all that we do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Fauveau, but I don't think we need to discuss it any further. Where is the new witness? Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm just switching.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will call the next witness. I have more time than is left today, so if Your Honours feel it best, we can start tomorrow morning. If, however, you wish us to start now, we are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the preliminaries at least. We'll clear those up. We'll clear those up, and then we can continue tomorrow if my colleagues are in agreement. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I welcome you to this Tribunal and to this case in particular where you are one of the witnesses summoned by the Defence team for Ljubisa Beara. You are about to start giving evidence now. We've only got 10 minutes left, and then we'll continue tomorrow. Before you start testifying, you are required by our rules to make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you'll be testifying the truth. The text is going to be handed to you now. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Since you were a judge in your career, you are perfectly aware what the procedure is likely to be here. The Beara Defence team who have summoned you as their witness will go first and direct examination of you; and they will then be followed by cross-examination from the Prosecution and possibly other Defence teams later on. Who is -- Mr. Nikolic. We finish at quarter to 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Medic. [Realtime transcript read in error, "Remetic"]

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Although we have been introduced, I will introduce myself officially now for the record. My name is Predrag Nikolic. I'm an attorney at law in the Defence team of Ljubisa Beara. Before you start answering my questions, we will have to agree on some technical matters. As we speak to each other in the Serbian language, the interpreters will need time to interpret all of this to the other participants in the courtroom. That's why I will ask you to always pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an error in the transcript. Page 75, line 21, it says Mr. Remetic; however, this gentleman is Mr. Medic. Mr. Remetic will arrive later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, for pointing that out, Mr. Nikolic. The correction will be effected in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, I will ask you now to introduce yourself to us. Tell us your first and last name and your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC
utterances.text: My name is Vojislav Medic. I was born on the 1st of October, 1956, in the village of Gornja Suvaja, Donji Lapac municipality. Now it is Gracac municipality in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your education?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC
utterances.text: I completed primary school, secondary military school, and the faculty of law at university.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you have any specialist education or training?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. After secondary school, I completed the course in radio telegraphy, and I sailed on submarines as a radio telegraph operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where have you worked as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC
utterances.text: After graduating from university in 1982, I was transferred to the military court in Ljubljana, where I was an intern for two years. After that in 1984, I was appointed an associate in the supreme military court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you volunteered to join the military legal service?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. After graduating from law school, I asked to be moved there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do? Did you deal with civil law or something else while you were in the army?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC
utterances.text: In the military, in the supreme military court, I was an associate in the crime department. In 1987, I was appointed an investigating judge in the investigating court in Belgrade military court, and I dealt only with criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And throughout this period until the outbreak of the war, were you an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC
utterances.text: Not throughout this period. I was an investigating judge from 1987 to 1993, if I remember correctly, and then I was the presiding judge of chambers sitting in criminal cases until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you to explain to us the organisation of the military courts in the period immediately preceding the outbreak of war, that is, up to 1992.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC
utterances.text: If you are referring to the territorial organisation, there were military courts attached to every military district. They used to be called armies. So every army had its own military court, and there was also a prosecutor's office, and then there was the supreme military court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you recall the names of these military courts and their headquarters, their seats, the first-instance military courts, that is?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC
utterances.text: Certainly. There was a military court in Belgrade for the 1st Army district; one in Ljubljana, I think it was the 9th army; one in Zagreb for the 2nd army; one in Split for the military naval district; one in Sarajevo, I think it was the 7th army; there was one in Skoplje; and I don't know what the number of that army was; and there was a military court in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This organisation of courts, was it changed and to what extent was it changed when Yugoslavia fell apart and when in 1992 the FRY was established? Can you explain the territorial organisation of the courts in the FRY as it was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC
utterances.text: I think that in 1991 or in 1992, I'm not exactly sure now, after the withdrawal of the army from Slovenia, the role of that court ceased to exist. There was a military court in Zagreb, but when war broke out the military court from Split was relocated to Tivat in Montenegro. The other courts continued working in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we could now finish for the day because I rounded off this topic and I intend to start a new one tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9:00.
